title: 3 Hours of AI Training (in Less Than 1,200 Words)
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews, writing for teachers under his 'Wise AI for Educators' banner, argues that durable AI guidance should focus on stable habits rather than tool-specific tips, since the underlying tools change constantly while the principles of good use do not. He lays out eight such habits: deciding ethical and practical no-go zones in advance, recognizing that AI saves time without automatically creating meaningful space (citing a 164,000-worker study showing AI users' deep focus time actually dropped), going deep with one tool rather than chasing every new app, writing structured Role/Task/Format prompts, iterating through conversation rather than expecting a perfect first output, protecting student and staff data ('never paste anything you wouldn't read aloud in a staff meeting'), sharing successful workflows across a school rather than letting excellence sit in silos, and noticing how heavy AI use reshapes one's own patience and expectations. Matthews frames all eight as decisions the individual teacher controls regardless of which specific AI product they use, comparing them to grammar, which persists across centuries of vocabulary change. The piece closes by asking readers what ninth habit they would add, positioning the list as a living framework rather than a finished one.
points: Cites a study of 164,000 workers showing AI users spent more time on email and reactive tasks while their deep focus time actually dropped, challenging the assumption that AI automatically frees up meaningful time.

Frames good AI use as durable habits (no-go zones, structured Role/Task/Format prompting, data discipline) rather than tool-specific tips, arguing habits transfer across tools the way grammar transfers across vocabulary change.
Recommends teachers go deep with one AI tool rather than chasing lists of 'fifty tools that will change your life,' arguing fluency transfers roughly 90% to the next tool anyway.
Highlights a data-privacy rule specific to school contexts: never paste student or staff information into an AI tool you would not be comfortable reading aloud in a staff meeting.
quotes: Almost nothing that makes AI use good or bad has to do with the tool itself. Swap Copilot for Claude, swap Claude for whatever hits our browsers in October, the same principles get you good results regardless of the tool.
A study of 164,000 workers found AI users spent more time on email and reactive tasks, and their deep focus time actually dropped.
Fluency in one tool beats a browser full of tabs you've only opened once.
Bad output is the result of bad input. As the data scientists say, "Garbage in, garbage out".

The simple rule: never paste anything into an AI tool you wouldn't be comfortable reading aloud in a staff meeting, because once the data toothpaste is out of the tube you don't get to decide where it goes.
Our tech shapes us. When I use AI a lot I can become impatient and easily frustrated.
